# American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2024
Organization: American Diabetes Association (ADA)
Publication Date: 2024-01-01
Document Version: 2024.1
Evidence Type: CLINICAL_GUIDELINE

metadata.document_title: Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2024
metadata.section_title: General Overview

chunks.text: Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) >= 126 mg/dL or HbA1c >= 6.5% establishes the diagnosis of Type 2 Diabetes. Prediabetes is defined by Fasting Plasma Glucose between 100 and 125 mg/dL or HbA1c between 5.7% and 6.4%. For non-pregnant adults with diabetes, a target HbA1c of < 7.0% is recommended to reduce microvascular complications.

metadata.document_title: Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2024
metadata.section_title: Section 1: Glycemic Targets and Diagnostic Criteria

chunks.text: Lifestyle behavior change is essential for diabetes prevention and management. Intensive lifestyle intervention targeting >= 7% weight loss through a low-calorie, low-fat diet and regular physical activity (at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise) reduces the risk of progressing from prediabetes to Type 2 Diabetes by 58%.

metadata.document_title: Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2024
metadata.section_title: Section 2: Lifestyle Modifications and Weight Management

chunks.text: Increased intake of dietary fiber (25–35 g/day from whole grains, legumes, vegetables, and fruit) improves glycemic control and insulin sensitivity. Viscous soluble fibers (e.g. beta-glucans, psyllium) delay gastric emptying and attenuate postprandial blood glucose spikes.

metadata.document_title: Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2024
metadata.section_title: Section 3: Dietary Fiber and Whole Foods

chunks.text: Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) telemetric metrics such as Time-in-Range (TIR > 70%), Glucose Variability (CV < 36%), and Average Daily Glucose offer actionable clinical insights for daily glycemic regulation. Patients with high glucose variability benefit from structured activity timing post-meals.

metadata.document_title: Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2024
metadata.section_title: Section 4: Physical Activity Telemetry and CGM Integration

# World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Obesity Prevention and Management
Organization: World Health Organization (WHO)
Publication Date: 2023-06-15
Document Version: 2023.2
Evidence Type: CLINICAL_GUIDELINE

metadata.document_title: Clinical Guidelines for Obesity Prevention and Management
metadata.section_title: General Overview

chunks.text: Obesity is classified as Body Mass Index (BMI) >= 30.0 kg/m2. Central adiposity, indicated by waist circumference >= 102 cm in men and >= 88 cm in women, significantly increases cardiovascular and metabolic risk independently of BMI.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Guidelines for Obesity Prevention and Management
metadata.section_title: Section 1: Classification and Adiposity Risk

chunks.text: Adults should engage in 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity per week. Wearable step telemetry indicates that increasing step count from 3,500 steps/day to 8,000–10,000 steps/day markedly reduces mortality and metabolic disease risk.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Guidelines for Obesity Prevention and Management
metadata.section_title: Section 2: Multimodal Physical Activity and Telemetry Guidelines

chunks.text: Reducing sedentary screen time (< 480 minutes/day) and maintaining optimal sleep duration (7 to 9 hours per night) are essential. Chronic short sleep (< 6 hours) impairs ghrelin/leptin regulation, increasing appetite and visceral fat deposition.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Guidelines for Obesity Prevention and Management
metadata.section_title: Section 3: Sedentary Behavior and Sleep Duration

# AASLD Practice Guidance on Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
Organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
Publication Date: 2023-12-01
Document Version: 2023.1
Evidence Type: CLINICAL_GUIDELINE

metadata.organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
metadata.document_title: Practice Guidance on Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
metadata.section_title: General Overview

chunks.text: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD / MASLD) risk is associated with hepatic steatosis, elevated liver enzymes (ALT > 35 U/L in males, > 25 U/L in females; AST), central obesity (BMI >= 28), elevated triglycerides (>= 150 mg/dL), and Type 2 Diabetes.

metadata.organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
metadata.document_title: Practice Guidance on Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
metadata.section_title: Section 1: Risk Assessment and Liver Biomarkers

chunks.text: A weight loss of 7% to 10% is recommended for patients with NAFLD to achieve steatosis reduction and resolution of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). A Mediterranean diet pattern, rich in monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA), omega-3 fatty acids, and low in refined sugars/fructose, is strongly recommended.

metadata.organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
metadata.document_title: Practice Guidance on Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
metadata.section_title: Section 2: Weight Reduction and Dietary Strategy

chunks.text: Substantial clinical evidence links gut microbial permeability and bacterial translocation to hepatic inflammation. Microbial fermentation products (Short-Chain Fatty Acids like butyrate and acetate) help maintain intestinal barrier integrity, dampening hepatic lipogenesis and systemic inflammation.

metadata.organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
metadata.document_title: Practice Guidance on Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
metadata.section_title: Section 3: Gut-Liver Axis and Metabolic Homeostasis

# AHA/NHLBI Diagnosis and Management of Metabolic Syndrome
Organization: American Heart Association / NHLBI
Publication Date: 2022-09-10
Document Version: 2022.1
Evidence Type: CLINICAL_GUIDELINE

metadata.document_title: Diagnosis and Management of the Metabolic Syndrome: An American Heart Association/National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Scientific Statement
metadata.section_title: General Overview

chunks.text:
Metabolic Syndrome is diagnosed when 3 or more of the following 5 criteria are present:
1. Elevated waist circumference (>= 102 cm men, >= 88 cm women)
2. Elevated triglycerides (>= 150 mg/dL)
3. Reduced HDL cholesterol (< 40 mg/dL men, < 50 mg/dL women)
4. Elevated blood pressure (Systolic >= 130 mmHg or Diastolic >= 85 mmHg)
5. Elevated fasting glucose (>= 100 mg/dL)

metadata.document_title: Diagnosis and Management of the Metabolic Syndrome: An American Heart Association/National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Scientific Statement
metadata.section_title: Section 1: ATP III Harmonized Diagnostic Criteria

chunks.text: First-line therapy focuses on lifestyle changes targeting atherogenic dyslipidemia, hypertension, and insulin resistance. Reducing saturated fats (< 7% of daily calories) and increasing physical activity reduces inflammatory markers (CRP, ALT).

metadata.document_title: Diagnosis and Management of the Metabolic Syndrome: An American Heart Association/National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Scientific Statement
metadata.section_title: Section 2: Clinical Management Strategy

# ISAPP Consensus Statement on Prebiotics, Dietary Fiber, and Short-Chain Fatty Acids
Organization: International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP)
Publication Date: 2023-04-20
Document Version: 2023.1
Evidence Type: EMERGING_RESEARCH

metadata.organization: International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP)
metadata.document_title: Consensus Statement on Prebiotics, Dietary Fiber, and Short-Chain Fatty Acids in Metabolic Health
metadata.section_title: General Overview

chunks.text: A prebiotic is defined as a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit. Prebiotic dietary fibers include galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS), fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS), inulin, and resistant starch found in legumes, oats, onions, garlic, and green bananas.

metadata.organization: International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP)
metadata.document_title: Consensus Statement on Prebiotics, Dietary Fiber, and Short-Chain Fatty Acids in Metabolic Health
metadata.section_title: Section 1: Prebiotic Definition and Dietary Fiber

chunks.text: Fermentation of dietary fibers by commensal taxa (such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia, and Akkermansia muciniphila) produces short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate). SCFA signaling via G-protein coupled receptors (GPR41/GPR43) stimulates GLP-1 and PYY secretion, enhancing satiety, insulin sensitivity, and liver fat regulation.

metadata.organization: International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP)
metadata.document_title: Consensus Statement on Prebiotics, Dietary Fiber, and Short-Chain Fatty Acids in Metabolic Health
metadata.section_title: Section 2: Microbial SCFA Production and Metabolic Health

chunks.text: Note: While observational studies link reduced levels of Akkermansia or Faecalibacterium with obesity, T2D, and NAFLD, current clinical evidence does not support targeted bacterial eradication or strain-specific medical prescription. General dietary fiber diversification (25–35 g/day) remains the evidence-grounded nutritional recommendation.

metadata.organization: International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP)
metadata.document_title: Consensus Statement on Prebiotics, Dietary Fiber, and Short-Chain Fatty Acids in Metabolic Health
metadata.section_title: Section 3: Observational Microbiome Association Safety Disclaimer
